summary: Defines binary formats for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selectors, which describe a particular flow of packets, for use with flow bindings in Mobile IPv6. A traffic selector lets a device say which traffic should be sent to which of its addresses. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic selector is a compact way of describing a flow of packets: the addresses, ports and other header values that traffic must have to belong to that flow. This document defines the binary layout of those selectors for IPv4 and for IPv6, so that a device and its home agent agree on how to read them.

questions: what is a binary traffic selector
how does an ipv6 traffic selector match a flow label
what are ts format values 1 and 2
subtitle: Compact binary formats for describing a flow of IPv4 or IPv6 packets, used by Mobile IPv6 flow bindings.

tldr.problem: Flow bindings in Mobile IPv6 need a way to say which packets belong to a flow, so that a device can steer different traffic to different addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6088 defines two binary traffic selector formats, one for IPv4 (TS Format 1) and one for IPv6 (TS Format 2). A set of flags says which fields are present, and most fields have a start and an optional end value to describe a range.
tldr.outcome: The selectors identify flows efficiently from well-known IP and transport header fields. RFC 6088 only defines the formats; the sub-option itself is in RFC 6089.

today: RFC 6088 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the formats for the traffic selector sub-option of RFC 6089.

sections.title: What the Document Defines
sections.content:
This document defines binary formats for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selector sub-options, as defined in RFC 6089.

The binary traffic selector format allows for efficient identification of flows based on well-known fields in the IPv4 and IPv6 headers and in transport layer headers such as TCP and UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is designed so that a receiver can pick out the packets of one conversation by looking at a few header fields, rather than by reading the packets themselves.

sections.title: Sub-Options and the TS Format Values
sections.content:
RFC 6089 defines the format of the traffic selector sub-option. This document defines two values of the TS Format field for binary traffic selectors: value 1 for the IPv4 binary traffic selector and value 2 for the IPv6 binary traffic selector.

Both formats share the same shape. They begin with the sub-option type, the sub-option length, the TS Format and a reserved octet, followed by a row of flag bits, one per optional field, and more reserved bits. Each flag says whether the matching field is present in the message, and every field that can be present has a start value and, in most cases, an end value that turns the start into a range.

Every end field MUST NOT be included unless the matching start field is included, and when the end field is present the receiver matches all the values between the start and the end, inclusive of both. The reserved bits MUST be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Both versions look the same: a header, a row of flags, then the values. A flag says the value is there, and an end value turns a single value into a range that includes both ends.

sections.title: The IPv4 Binary Traffic Selector
sections.content:
When the TS Format field indicates the IPv4 binary traffic selector, the sub-option is laid out as shown in Figure 1 of the document, with the alignment requirement of 4n if any of the flags A, B, C, D, E or F is set, 2n if any of G, H, I or J is set, and n if any of K, L, M or N is set.

Flag A is the start source address, which identifies the first of the 32-bit IPv4 addresses to be matched on data packets sent from a corresponding node to the mobile node as seen by the home agent, in other words one of the addresses of the correspondent node. Flag B is the end source address, used when more than one contiguous source address has to be matched. Flag C is the start destination address, one of the registered home addresses of the mobile node, and flag D is its matching end value.

Flag E is the start IPsec SPI, the Security Parameter Index, which is a 32-bit value, and flag F is the end SPI value. The SPI is defined in RFC 4303.

Flag G is the start source port, a 16-bit port number from the range assigned by IANA, and flag H is the end source port. Flag I is the start destination port and flag J is the end destination port.

Flag K is the start differential services value, and flag L is the end value. This field is called the Type of Service field in RFC 791, which RFC 3260 later clarified as a 6-bit DS field with 2 bits reserved, later claimed by Explicit Congestion Notification. For this specification the field is 8 bits long, where the 6 most significant bits indicate the DS field to be matched and the 2 least significant bits MUST be ignored in any comparison.

Flag M is the start protocol value, an 8-bit value, and flag N is the end protocol value.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 selector can match on the source and destination addresses, the IPsec security parameter index, the source and destination ports, the differentiated services value and the protocol number. Each one can be a single value or a range, and the flags say which ones are in use.

sections.title: The IPv6 Binary Traffic Selector
sections.content:
When the TS Format field indicates the IPv6 binary traffic selector, the sub-option is laid out as shown in Figure 2, with the alignment requirement of 8n if any of A, B, C or D is set, 4n if any of E, F, G or H is set, 2n if any of I, J, K or L is set, and n if any of M, N, O or P is set.

Flags A to D are the start and end source and destination addresses, this time 128-bit IPv6 addresses, with the same meaning as in the IPv4 selector: the source is one of the addresses of the correspondent node and the destination is one of the registered home addresses of the mobile node.

Flags E and F are the start and end IPsec SPI values, both 32 bits. Flags G and H are the start and end flow label values. The flow label is 24 bits long according to RFC 2460, and for this specification the sender of the option MUST prefix the flow label value with 8 bits of zero before inserting it, while the receiver SHOULD ignore the first 8 bits of the field before comparing it with flow labels in packets.

Flags I to L are the start and end source and destination ports, 16 bits each. Flags M and N are the start and end traffic class values, which are equivalent to the start and end DS fields of the IPv4 selector: 8 bits long, with the 6 most significant bits indicating the DS field to be matched and the 2 least significant bits ignored in any comparison. Flags O and P are the start and end next header values, 8 bits each.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 selector matches on the same kinds of values plus the flow label, and uses the next header field where IPv4 uses the protocol field. The 24-bit flow label is stored in a 32-bit field with eight leading zero bits, and the receiver is told to ignore those bits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document defines the format of the traffic selector field of a sub-option defined for flow bindings in RFC 6089. The authors have not identified any security concerns pertaining to this document beyond what is already identified in RFC 6089.
sections.plainLanguage: Defining the fields adds no new risk of its own; the security questions sit with the flow binding mechanism the fields belong to.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Two new TS format values have been assigned from the Traffic Selector Format namespace for the traffic selector sub-option defined in RFC 6089: value 1 for the IPv4 binary traffic selector and value 2 for the IPv6 binary traffic selector.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers are registered to say which of the two layouts is in use.
